items.stem: Define the term "compound".
items.answer: A substance made of two or more different elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a substance made of two or more different elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between simple distillation and fractional distillation.
items.answer: Simple distillation separates a volatile liquid from dissolved solids (or liquids with very different boiling points); fractional distillation uses a fractionating column to separate miscible liquids with close boiling points.
items.markingKey: Simple distillation separates a volatile liquid from dissolved solids (or liquids with very different boiling points); fractional distillation uses a fractionating column to separate miscible liquids with close boiling points. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Distillation works because the solid has a higher density than the liquid." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Distillation depends on a difference in volatility (boiling point), not density; the liquid vaporises and condenses while the non-volatile solute remains.
items.markingKey: Distillation depends on a difference in volatility (boiling point), not density; the liquid vaporises and condenses while the non-volatile solute remains. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Chloé repeated a paper chromatography experiment to check the reproducibility of a dye spot. The repeated readings of the distance moved by a dye spot were 7.5, 7.6, 7.4 cm. Calculate the mean and its absolute uncertainty.
items.markingKey: Mean = 7.5 cm (A1); uncertainty = half the range = (7.6 − 7.4)/2 = 0.1 cm (A1).

items.stem: Suggest how pure water from ink could be separated in the laboratory, explaining why the method works.
items.answer: Simple distillation: water is volatile while the dyes are not.
items.markingKey: Technique: simple distillation (1); property/explanation: water is volatile while the dyes are not (1).

items.stem:
A student analysed a sweet coating by paper chromatography using a water/ethanol solvent. The solvent front travelled 10.7 cm. Two spots appeared at 2.8 cm and 6.5 cm from the base line. Reference dyes run under identical conditions gave:
E102 (tartrazine): Rf = 0.27
E129 (allura red): Rf = 0.49
E133 (brilliant blue): Rf = 0.61

(a) Calculate the Rf value of each spot. [2]
(b) Deduce which dyes are present in the coating. [1]
(c) The ruler has a precision of ±0.1 cm. Determine the percentage uncertainty in the Rf value of the lower spot. [2]
(d) Explain why the beaker was covered with a lid while the chromatogram developed. [2]
(e) Suggest why a second, different solvent should be used before drawing a firm conclusion. [1]
items.answer: (a) 0.26 and 0.61 (b) E102 (tartrazine) and E133 (brilliant blue) (c) 4.5 % (d) To saturate the air with solvent vapour so the solvent does not evaporate from the paper and the solvent front rises evenly. (e) Different dyes may have the same Rf in one solvent; agreement in two solvents is much stronger evidence.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] Rf = distance moved by spot / distance moved by solvent front (M1); 0.26 and 0.61 (A1). (b) [1] E102 (tartrazine) and E133 (brilliant blue) – closest Rf values (A1). (c) [2] % uncertainty = 0.1/2.8 × 100 + 0.1/10.7 × 100 (M1) = 4.5 % (A1). (d) [2] Prevents evaporation of the solvent from the paper / keeps atmosphere saturated (1); gives reproducible Rf values (1). (e) [1] Coincident Rf in one solvent possible (1).

items.stem: Classify each of the following as an element, a compound or a mixture (state whether any mixture is homogeneous or heterogeneous): milk; glucose; graphite.
items.answer: milk: mixture – heterogeneous (colloid); glucose: compound; graphite: element
items.markingKey: milk: mixture – heterogeneous (colloid); glucose: compound; graphite: element (1 mark per correct classification).

items.stem: Why is a fractionating column packed with glass beads?
options: to absorb water from the vapour
to provide a large surface area for repeated condensation and vaporisation
to cool the vapour quickly to room temperature
items.answer: to provide a large surface area for repeated condensation and vaporisation
items.markingKey: B. Many condensation-vaporisation cycles enrich the vapour in the more volatile component.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the solvent front must be marked as soon as a chromatogram is removed from the tank.
items.answer: The solvent evaporates quickly and the front becomes invisible; its position is needed to calculate Rf = distance moved by spot / distance moved by solvent.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The solvent evaporates quickly and the front becomes invisible; its position is needed to calculate Rf = distance moved by spot / distance moved by solvent. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A sample of a white solid melts over the range 118–123 °C. The literature melting point of the pure substance is 122 °C. What does this suggest?
options: The sample is a compound, not an element.
items.answer: The sample is impure.
items.markingKey: B. Impurities lower and broaden the melting range.

items.stem: Rafael obtained a chromatogram on which a blue ink component had an Rf value of 0.47. The solvent front was 7.8 cm above the base line. Determine how far the spot travelled.
items.answer: 3.7 cm
items.markingKey: C. distance = Rf × solvent front distance = 0.47 × 7.8 (M1) = 3.7 cm (A1).

items.stem: A student needs to obtain nitrogen and oxygen from liquefied air. Which method should be used?
items.answer: fractional distillation
items.markingKey: B. Fractional distillation: N₂ (−196 °C) and O₂ (−183 °C) have different boiling points.

items.stem: Kwame obtained a chromatogram on which a yellow pigment from a highlighter had an Rf value of 0.54. The solvent front was 8.1 cm above the base line. Determine how far the spot travelled.
items.answer: 4.4 cm
items.markingKey: distance = Rf × solvent front distance = 0.54 × 8.1 (M1) = 4.4 cm (A1).

items.stem: Plan an investigation, using paper chromatography, to find out whether an orange drink contains the dye E110 (sunset yellow). Include the procedure, how the results would be analysed and one limitation.
items.answer: Draw a pencil base line; spot the drink extract and a reference sample of E110 side by side; place in a tank with solvent below the line; cover; remove when the solvent front is near the top and mark it; calculate Rf values. Same Rf and colour as the reference suggests E110 is present. Limitation: another dye could share the Rf – repeat with a different solvent.
items.markingKey: Draw a pencil base line; spot the drink extract and a reference sample of E110 side by side; place in a tank with solvent below the line; cover; remove when the solvent front is near the top and mark it; calculate Rf values. Same Rf and colour as the reference suggests E110 is present. Limitation: another dye could share the Rf – repeat with a different solvent.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "kinetic molecular theory"?
options: Two or more substances physically combined in variable proportions and not chemically bonded
The temperature at which the solid and liquid states of a pure substance are in equilibrium at a given pressure
A substance made of two or more different elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio
The model in which matter consists of particles in constant random motion whose average kinetic energy is proportional to the absolute temperature
items.answer: The model in which matter consists of particles in constant random motion whose average kinetic energy is proportional to the absolute temperature
items.markingKey: D. "kinetic molecular theory" is the model in which matter consists of particles in constant random motion whose average kinetic energy is proportional to the absolute temperature.

items.stem: Explain the difference between deposition and sublimation.
items.answer: Sublimation is solid → gas (endothermic); deposition is gas → solid (exothermic).
items.markingKey: Sublimation is solid → gas (endothermic); deposition is gas → solid (exothermic). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "At 0 °C the particles of a substance stop moving." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Particles have minimum kinetic energy only at absolute zero (0 K = −273 °C); at 0 °C (273 K) they still vibrate/move.
items.markingKey: Particles have minimum kinetic energy only at absolute zero (0 K = −273 °C); at 0 °C (273 K) they still vibrate/move. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A pure sample of benzene is heated at a constant rate from −34 °C to 90 °C. The temperature–time graph shows two horizontal sections. State the temperatures of the two horizontal sections and explain why the second horizontal section is longer than the first.
items.answer: 6 °C (melting) and 80 °C (boiling); boiling requires the intermolecular attractions to be overcome completely so far more energy (time) is needed than for melting.
items.markingKey: 6 °C and 80 °C (1); energy used to overcome attractions, temperature constant (1); vaporisation separates particles completely – greater enthalpy change than fusion (1).

items.stem: The melting point of methane is 91 K and its boiling point is 111 K. Deduce the physical state of methane at −151 °C, showing your reasoning.
items.markingKey: Converts −151 °C to 122 K (M1); compares with 91 K and 111 K to give gas (A1).

items.stem:
A student analysed a sweet coating by paper chromatography using a water/ethanol solvent. The solvent front travelled 8.6 cm. Two spots appeared at 3.5 cm and 6.0 cm from the base line. Reference dyes run under identical conditions gave:
E102 (tartrazine): Rf = 0.26
E129 (allura red): Rf = 0.42
E133 (brilliant blue): Rf = 0.70

(a) Calculate the Rf value of each spot. [2]
(b) Deduce which dyes are present in the coating. [1]
(c) The ruler has a precision of ±0.1 cm. Determine the percentage uncertainty in the Rf value of the lower spot. [2]
(d) Explain why the beaker was covered with a lid while the chromatogram developed. [2]
(e) Suggest why a second, different solvent should be used before drawing a firm conclusion. [1]
items.answer: (a) 0.41 and 0.70 (b) E129 (allura red) and E133 (brilliant blue) (c) 4.0 % (d) To saturate the air with solvent vapour so the solvent does not evaporate from the paper and the solvent front rises evenly. (e) Different dyes may have the same Rf in one solvent; agreement in two solvents is much stronger evidence.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] Rf = distance moved by spot / distance moved by solvent front (M1); 0.41 and 0.70 (A1). (b) [1] E129 (allura red) and E133 (brilliant blue) – closest Rf values (A1). (c) [2] % uncertainty = 0.1/3.5 × 100 + 0.1/8.6 × 100 (M1) = 4.0 % (A1). (d) [2] Prevents evaporation of the solvent from the paper / keeps atmosphere saturated (1); gives reproducible Rf values (1). (e) [1] Coincident Rf in one solvent possible (1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The temperature at which the solid and liquid states of a pure substance are in equilibrium at a given pressure"?
items.answer: melting point
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of melting point.

items.stem: Why does the temperature of a liquid stay constant while it boils at constant pressure?
options: The particles lose kinetic energy to the walls.
Energy is used to separate the particles rather than increase their kinetic energy.
items.answer: Energy is used to separate the particles rather than increase their kinetic energy.
items.markingKey: D. Latent heat increases potential energy.

items.stem: Explain why a gas spreads to fill its container (diffuses).
items.answer: Gas particles move rapidly and randomly with negligible attractions between them, so they spread from regions of high concentration until evenly distributed.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Gas particles move rapidly and randomly with negligible attractions between them, so they spread from regions of high concentration until evenly distributed. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Diego writes: "When ice melts the water molecules break into hydrogen and oxygen atoms." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Melting only overcomes intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds) between molecules; the covalent O–H bonds within molecules remain intact.
items.markingKey: Melting only overcomes intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds) between molecules; the covalent O–H bonds within molecules remain intact. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The temperature of a sample of helium gas is raised from −73 °C to 373 °C. By what factor does the average kinetic energy of the particles increase?
items.markingKey: B. Ek ∝ T/K: (373 + 273)/(−73 + 273) = 3.23. Using Celsius values is the common error.

items.stem:
The mass spectrum of a sample of gallium gave the following peaks (singly charged ions only):
m/z 69 | relative peak height 100.0
m/z 71 | relative peak height 66.4

(a) Calculate the percentage abundance of each isotope. [2]
(b) Calculate the relative atomic mass of the sample to two decimal places. [2]
(c) Identify the element from its relative atomic mass and state one reason why the value may differ slightly from the data booklet value. [2]
(d) Explain why the sample must be ionised before it can be analysed. [1]
(e) State why a small peak at half the m/z of the most abundant isotope could appear. [1]
items.answer: (a) 69: 60.1 %, 71: 39.9 % (b) 69.80 (c) gallium; isotopic abundances vary slightly between natural sources / peak-height measurement uncertainty. (d) Only charged particles can be accelerated and deflected (separated) by electric/magnetic fields and detected. (e) Formation of 2+ ions, which have half the m/z value.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] Each height ÷ sum of heights × 100 (M1); correct percentages (A1). (b) [2] Σ(m/z × height)/Σheights (M1) = 69.80 (A1). (c) [2] gallium (1); valid reason (1). (d) [1] Ions are accelerated/deflected/detected (1). (e) [1] 2+ ions (1).

items.stem: "The kinetic molecular theory is a good model for explaining the behaviour of all states of matter." Discuss.
items.answer: It is a powerful qualitative model, especially for gases, but has limited predictive power for condensed phases – models are simplifications (NOS).
items.markingKey: Arguments for: explains diffusion, pressure, changes of state and the effect of temperature; links macroscopic temperature to particle kinetic energy. Arguments against: treats particles as simple spheres and ignores the details of bonding; does not quantitatively predict properties of liquids and solids; cannot explain quantum effects at very low temperatures. Supported judgement: It is a powerful qualitative model, especially for gases, but has limited predictive power for condensed phases – models are simplifications (NOS). Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: A heating curve is obtained for a pure sample of ethanol heated from −130 °C to 100 °C (melting point −114 °C, boiling point 78 °C). Sketch and describe the curve, explaining each section in terms of particles and energy.
items.answer: Rising section (solid warming: vibrations increase); plateau at −114 °C (melting: energy overcomes attractions, temperature constant); rising section (liquid warming); longer plateau at 78 °C (boiling: particles separate completely); rising section (gas warming). Gradients depend on heat capacities.
items.markingKey: Rising section (solid warming: vibrations increase); plateau at −114 °C (melting: energy overcomes attractions, temperature constant); rising section (liquid warming); longer plateau at 78 °C (boiling: particles separate completely); rising section (gas warming). Gradients depend on heat capacities.

items.stem: Which particles are found in the nucleus of an atom?
items.answer: protons and neutrons
items.markingKey: protons and neutrons. The nucleus contains the nucleons.

items.stem: Which statement about the ¹H, ²H and ³H isotopes is correct?
options: They each have one proton but different numbers of neutrons.
Only ¹H is an isotope of hydrogen.
They have different numbers of electrons.
items.answer: They each have one proton but different numbers of neutrons.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an ion and an atom.
items.answer: An atom is neutral (protons = electrons); an ion is charged because it has lost or gained electrons.
items.markingKey: An atom is neutral (protons = electrons); an ion is charged because it has lost or gained electrons. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using cobalt-60 used to sterilise surgical equipment as an example, explain applications of radioisotopes.
items.answer: Gamma rays from ⁶⁰Co kill bacteria on packaged instruments. Highly penetrating gamma radiation from an unstable nucleus can sterilise without heating.
items.markingKey: Context (Gamma rays from ⁶⁰Co kill bacteria on packaged instruments.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Highly penetrating gamma radiation from an unstable nucleus can sterilise without heating. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to applications of radioisotopes.

items.stem: "The mass number is the number of neutrons in the nucleus." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The mass number is protons + neutrons; neutrons = A − Z.
items.markingKey: The mass number is protons + neutrons; neutrons = A − Z. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which atom contains the largest number of neutrons? (Atomic numbers: Ca 20, C 6, Cu 29, Ti 22)
items.answer: ⁶³Cu
items.markingKey: A. ⁶³Cu has 34 neutrons (A − Z).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The use of radioisotopes in medicine brings more benefits than risks."
items.answer: With careful choice of isotope (short half-life, appropriate radiation) and dose control the benefits generally outweigh the risks.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: diagnosis with tracers (Tc-99m) is non-invasive; targeted therapy (I-131) treats cancers effectively; short half-lives limit exposure. Arguments against: ionising radiation can damage healthy cells and DNA; risks to staff and in disposal of waste; production requires nuclear reactors. Supported judgement: With careful choice of isotope (short half-life, appropriate radiation) and dose control the benefits generally outweigh the risks.

items.stem: Gallium has two stable isotopes, ⁶⁹Ga and ⁷¹Ga. (a) State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in a ⁷¹Ga³⁺ ion. (b) Explain why the two isotopes react identically with hydrochloric acid. (c) Suggest one physical property that would differ between samples of the pure isotopes.
items.answer: (a) 31 p, 40 n, 28 e; (b) same electron configuration/same number of electrons; (c) density (or rate of diffusion, melting point slightly).
items.markingKey: (a) 31 p, 40 n, 28 e; (b) same electron configuration/same number of electrons; (c) density (or rate of diffusion, melting point slightly).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "ion"?
options: The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom
Two or more substances physically combined in variable proportions and not chemically bonded
A substance made of two or more different elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio
A charged particle formed when an atom or group of atoms loses or gains electrons
items.answer: A charged particle formed when an atom or group of atoms loses or gains electrons
items.markingKey: D. "ion" is a charged particle formed when an atom or group of atoms loses or gains electrons.

items.stem: Which property differs between ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl atoms?
items.answer: density of the gas
items.markingKey: B. Isotopes differ in mass-dependent physical properties such as density and rate of diffusion.

items.stem: Explain why an atom is electrically neutral.
items.answer: It contains equal numbers of protons (each +1) and electrons (each −1), so the charges cancel.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It contains equal numbers of protons (each +1) and electrons (each −1), so the charges cancel. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between an atom and an ion.
items.answer: An atom is neutral (protons = electrons); an ion is charged because it has lost or gained electrons.
items.markingKey: An atom is neutral (protons = electrons); an ion is charged because it has lost or gained electrons. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A species contains 6 protons, 7 neutrons and 6 electrons. Identify the species, giving its nuclear symbol with mass number.
items.answer: ¹³C
items.markingKey: Element from Z = 6: C (1); mass number 13 = 6 + 7 (1); neutral as p = e (1).

items.stem: How many electrons and neutrons are present in ⁴⁴Ca²⁺? (Z = 20)
items.answer: 18 electrons, 24 neutrons
items.markingKey: D. electrons = 20 − (2) = 18; neutrons = 44 − 20 = 24.

items.stem: How many electrons and neutrons are present in ¹⁰⁷Ag⁺? (Z = 47)
items.answer: 46 electrons, 60 neutrons

items.stem: In a mass spectrum of an element, what does the height of each peak represent?
options: the number of neutrons in the isotope
the relative abundance of that isotope
items.answer: the relative abundance of that isotope
items.markingKey: B. Peak height ∝ number of ions of that m/z.

items.stem: Distinguish between relative isotopic mass and relative atomic mass.
items.answer: Relative isotopic mass is the mass of one isotope relative to 1/12 of ¹²C; relative atomic mass is the abundance-weighted mean of the isotopic masses of the element.
items.markingKey: Relative isotopic mass is the mass of one isotope relative to 1/12 of ¹²C; relative atomic mass is the abundance-weighted mean of the isotopic masses of the element. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A mass spectrum of an element shows peaks at m/z 24 (79 %), 25 (10 %) and 26 (11 %). What is the element?
items.answer: magnesium
items.markingKey: B. Ar ≈ 24.3 – magnesium.

items.stem: A student claims: "In the mass spectrum of chlorine the peak at m/z 37 is the tallest because ³⁷Cl is heavier." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Peak height shows abundance, not mass: the ³⁵Cl peak is about three times taller because ³⁵Cl is about 75 % of chlorine atoms.
items.markingKey: Peak height shows abundance, not mass: the ³⁵Cl peak is about three times taller because ³⁵Cl is about 75 % of chlorine atoms. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The relative atomic mass of a sample of gallium is 69.80. The sample contains only ⁶⁹Ga and ⁷¹Ga. Determine the percentage of ⁶⁹Ga atoms in the sample.
items.answer: ⁶⁹Ga 60.0 %, ⁷¹Ga 40.0 %

items.answer: relative atomic mass (Ar)

items.stem: Explain why relative atomic masses have no units.
items.answer: They are ratios: the mean mass of an atom divided by one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, so the units cancel.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They are ratios: the mean mass of an atom divided by one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, so the units cancel. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "The relative atomic mass of an element is the mass number of its most common isotope." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Ar is the weighted mean of all isotopes present, so it is usually not a whole number (e.g. Cl 35.45, not 35).
items.markingKey: Ar is the weighted mean of all isotopes present, so it is usually not a whole number (e.g. Cl 35.45, not 35). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A sample of lithium from a mineral has the following isotopic composition: ⁶Li 7.59 %, ⁷Li 92.41 %. What is the relative atomic mass of Li in this sample to two decimal places.
items.markingKey: A. Ar = Σ(mass × abundance)/100 = 6.92. A simple mean of the masses (6.50) ignores abundance.

items.stem: A sample of silver analysed in a geology laboratory has the following isotopic composition: ¹⁰⁷Ag 53.4 %, ¹⁰⁹Ag 46.6 %. Calculate the relative atomic mass of Ag in this sample to two decimal places.
A sample of iridium from a mineral has the following isotopic composition: ¹⁹¹Ir 37.3 %, ¹⁹³Ir 62.7 %. Calculate the relative atomic mass of Ir in this sample to two decimal places.
"Relative atomic masses quoted to two decimal places in the data booklet are exact constants of nature." Discuss.
items.answer: They are conventional representative values; small natural variations mean they are not exact constants, which matters in high-precision work.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they are measured very precisely by mass spectrometry; used consistently in calculations worldwide. Arguments against: isotopic abundances vary slightly with the source of a sample (e.g. boron, lead); IUPAC now gives some Ar values as intervals; precision is limited by measurement. Supported judgement: They are conventional representative values; small natural variations mean they are not exact constants, which matters in high-precision work. items.stem: A sample of bromine contains 50 % ⁷⁹Br and 50 % ⁸¹Br. (a) State the m/z values of the molecular-ion peaks expected for Br₂⁺. (b) Calculate the relative heights of these peaks, taking the tallest as 100. (c) Calculate Ar for this sample.
Which term matches this description: "Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons"?
items.answer: isotopes
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of isotopes.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "compound"?
options: Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
A substance made of two or more different elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio
A mixture with uniform composition and properties throughout, in a single phase
The temperature at which the solid and liquid states of a pure substance are in equilibrium at a given pressure
items.answer: A substance made of two or more different elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio
items.markingKey: B. "compound" is a substance made of two or more different elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio.

items.stem: Which describes the particles in a liquid?
options: close together, irregularly arranged and able to move past each other
far apart and moving rapidly in straight lines
in fixed positions in a regular lattice
items.answer: close together, irregularly arranged and able to move past each other
items.markingKey: A. Liquids: close-packed, disordered, particles can slide past one another.

items.stem: Explain the difference between relative isotopic mass and relative atomic mass.
items.answer: Relative isotopic mass is the mass of one isotope relative to 1/12 of ¹²C; relative atomic mass is the abundance-weighted mean of the isotopic masses of the element.
items.markingKey: Relative isotopic mass is the mass of one isotope relative to 1/12 of ¹²C; relative atomic mass is the abundance-weighted mean of the isotopic masses of the element. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Which pair of species has the same number of electrons?
items.answer: Na⁺ and F⁻
items.markingKey: A. Both have 10 electrons (isoelectronic).

items.stem: Explain the difference between fractional distillation and simple distillation.
items.answer: Simple distillation separates a volatile liquid from dissolved solids (or liquids with very different boiling points); fractional distillation uses a fractionating column to separate miscible liquids with close boiling points.
items.markingKey: Simple distillation separates a volatile liquid from dissolved solids (or liquids with very different boiling points); fractional distillation uses a fractionating column to separate miscible liquids with close boiling points. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between deposition and sublimation.
items.answer: Sublimation is solid → gas (endothermic); deposition is gas → solid (exothermic).
items.markingKey: Sublimation is solid → gas (endothermic); deposition is gas → solid (exothermic). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the relative atomic mass of copper (63.55) is closer to 63 than to 65.
items.answer: Copper consists of ⁶³Cu and ⁶⁵Cu; the weighted mean lies closer to 63 because ⁶³Cu is the more abundant isotope (about 69 %).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Copper consists of ⁶³Cu and ⁶⁵Cu; the weighted mean lies closer to 63 because ⁶³Cu is the more abundant isotope (about 69 %). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "The mass number is the number of neutrons in the nucleus." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The mass number is protons + neutrons; neutrons = A − Z.
items.markingKey: The mass number is protons + neutrons; neutrons = A − Z. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe forensic analysis of ink from a forged cheque using paper chromatography and explain what it reveals about identification of components using Rf values.
items.answer: The ink is spotted beside inks from suspects' pens and the chromatogram developed in the same solvent. Matching patterns of spots with identical Rf values under identical conditions links the ink to a pen.
items.markingKey: Context (The ink is spotted beside inks from suspects' pens and the chromatogram developed in the same solvent.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Matching patterns of spots with identical Rf values under identical conditions links the ink to a pen. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to identification of components using Rf values.

items.stem: A pure sample of benzene is heated at a constant rate from −14 °C to 100 °C. The temperature–time graph shows two horizontal sections. State the temperatures of the two horizontal sections and explain why the second horizontal section is longer than the first.
items.answer: 6 °C (melting) and 80 °C (boiling); boiling requires the intermolecular attractions to be overcome completely so far more energy (time) is needed than for melting.
items.markingKey: 6 °C and 80 °C (1); energy used to overcome attractions, temperature constant (1); vaporisation separates particles completely – greater enthalpy change than fusion (1).

items.answer: ¹³¹I

items.stem: "Elements are always made of single, separate atoms." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Many elements exist as molecules (O₂, Cl₂, P₄, S₈) or giant structures (diamond, metals); an element simply contains only one type of atom.
items.markingKey: Many elements exist as molecules (O₂, Cl₂, P₄, S₈) or giant structures (diamond, metals); an element simply contains only one type of atom. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
A student analysed a sweet coating by paper chromatography using a water/ethanol solvent. The solvent front travelled 9.1 cm. Two spots appeared at 2.5 cm and 6.2 cm from the base line. Reference dyes run under identical conditions gave:
E102 (tartrazine): Rf = 0.29
E129 (allura red): Rf = 0.49
E133 (brilliant blue): Rf = 0.68

(a) Calculate the Rf value of each spot. [2]
(b) Deduce which dyes are present in the coating. [1]
(c) The ruler has a precision of ±0.1 cm. Determine the percentage uncertainty in the Rf value of the lower spot. [2]
(d) Explain why the beaker was covered with a lid while the chromatogram developed. [2]
(e) Suggest why a second, different solvent should be used before drawing a firm conclusion. [1]
items.answer: (a) 0.27 and 0.68 (b) E102 (tartrazine) and E133 (brilliant blue) (c) 5.1 % (d) To saturate the air with solvent vapour so the solvent does not evaporate from the paper and the solvent front rises evenly. (e) Different dyes may have the same Rf in one solvent; agreement in two solvents is much stronger evidence.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] Rf = distance moved by spot / distance moved by solvent front (M1); 0.27 and 0.68 (A1). (b) [1] E102 (tartrazine) and E133 (brilliant blue) – closest Rf values (A1). (c) [2] % uncertainty = 0.1/2.5 × 100 + 0.1/9.1 × 100 (M1) = 5.1 % (A1). (d) [2] Prevents evaporation of the solvent from the paper / keeps atmosphere saturated (1); gives reproducible Rf values (1). (e) [1] Coincident Rf in one solvent possible (1).

items.stem: Europium has two isotopes, ¹⁵¹Eu and ¹⁵³Eu, and a relative atomic mass of 152.04. Calculate the percentage abundance of each isotope.
items.answer: ¹⁵¹Eu 48.0 %, ¹⁵³Eu 52.0 %

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "The use of radioisotopes in medicine brings more benefits than risks."
items.answer: With careful choice of isotope (short half-life, appropriate radiation) and dose control the benefits generally outweigh the risks.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: diagnosis with tracers (Tc-99m) is non-invasive; targeted therapy (I-131) treats cancers effectively; short half-lives limit exposure. Arguments against: ionising radiation can damage healthy cells and DNA; risks to staff and in disposal of waste; production requires nuclear reactors. Supported judgement: With careful choice of isotope (short half-life, appropriate radiation) and dose control the benefits generally outweigh the risks.

items.stem: "Paper chromatography is a sufficient technique to prove that a food colouring contains only permitted dyes." Discuss.
items.answer: Chromatography is a useful screening method, but proof requires matching in more than one solvent system and ideally an instrumental method.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it is cheap, quick and needs only a tiny sample; matching Rf values with reference dyes is good evidence. Arguments against: two different dyes may have the same Rf in one solvent; Rf depends on conditions and colourless components are invisible; confirmatory techniques (two solvents, HPLC, mass spectrometry) are needed for proof. Supported judgement: Chromatography is a useful screening method, but proof requires matching in more than one solvent system and ideally an instrumental method. items.stem: "The kinetic molecular theory is a good model for explaining the behaviour of all states of matter." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: It is a powerful qualitative model, especially for gases, but has limited predictive power for condensed phases – models are simplifications (NOS).
items.markingKey: Arguments for: explains diffusion, pressure, changes of state and the effect of temperature; links macroscopic temperature to particle kinetic energy. Arguments against: treats particles as simple spheres and ignores the details of bonding; does not quantitatively predict properties of liquids and solids; cannot explain quantum effects at very low temperatures. Supported judgement: It is a powerful qualitative model, especially for gases, but has limited predictive power for condensed phases – models are simplifications (NOS). items.stem: Deduce the numbers of subatomic particles in the species Zn-64. The atomic number of Zn is 30.
items.answer: 30 protons, 34 neutrons, 30 electrons
items.markingKey: p = Z = 30; n = A − Z = 64 − 30 = 34; e = 30 − (0) = 30. (2 marks for all three correct, 1 mark for two.)

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The component of a solution, usually present in the larger amount, in which the solute dissolves"?

items.stem: Explain why almost all the mass of an atom is concentrated in its nucleus.
items.answer: Protons and neutrons each have a relative mass of about 1, whereas electrons have a relative mass of only about 1/1840.

items.stem: "A substance with a high Rf value is more strongly attracted to the paper." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A high Rf means the substance moved further with the solvent: it is more attracted to the mobile phase (more soluble in the solvent) and less to the stationary phase.
items.markingKey: A high Rf means the substance moved further with the solvent: it is more attracted to the mobile phase (more soluble in the solvent) and less to the stationary phase. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Two gases are at the same temperature. Which quantity must be the same for both?
options: the average speed of the particles
the average kinetic energy of the particles
items.answer: the average kinetic energy of the particles
items.markingKey: D. Average Ek depends only on T; lighter particles move faster.

items.stem: With reference to the extraction of salt from rock salt, explain how it illustrates combining dissolving, filtration and crystallisation.

items.answer: gas

items.stem: The temperature of a sample of neon gas is raised from 27 °C to 127 °C. By what factor does the average kinetic energy of the particles increase?
items.markingKey: D. Ek ∝ T/K: (127 + 273)/(27 + 273) = 1.33. Using Celsius values is the common error.

items.stem:
The mass spectrum of a sample of copper gave the following peaks (singly charged ions only):
m/z 63 | relative peak height 100.0
m/z 65 | relative peak height 44.6

(a) Calculate the percentage abundance of each isotope. [2]
(b) Calculate the relative atomic mass of the sample to two decimal places. [2]
(c) Identify the element from its relative atomic mass and state one reason why the value may differ slightly from the data booklet value. [2]
(d) Explain why the sample must be ionised before it can be analysed. [1]
(e) State why a small peak at half the m/z of the most abundant isotope could appear. [1]
items.answer: (a) 63: 69.2 %, 65: 30.8 % (b) 63.62 (c) copper; isotopic abundances vary slightly between natural sources / peak-height measurement uncertainty. (d) Only charged particles can be accelerated and deflected (separated) by electric/magnetic fields and detected. (e) Formation of 2+ ions, which have half the m/z value.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] Each height ÷ sum of heights × 100 (M1); correct percentages (A1). (b) [2] Σ(m/z × height)/Σheights (M1) = 63.62 (A1). (c) [2] copper (1); valid reason (1). (d) [1] Ions are accelerated/deflected/detected (1). (e) [1] 2+ ions (1).

items.stem: "Distillation is the best way to provide drinking water for a coastal city." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Distillation is effective but costly; the best choice depends on available energy (e.g. waste heat or solar), with reverse osmosis often preferred.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: produces very pure water from an unlimited source; reliable and independent of rainfall. Arguments against: very high energy demand and associated CO₂ emissions; brine waste harms marine ecosystems; reverse osmosis is usually cheaper per m³. Supported judgement: Distillation is effective but costly; the best choice depends on available energy (e.g. waste heat or solar), with reverse osmosis often preferred.
